title: Equal Groups
big_idea: Same-size groups can be counted fast
child_idea: Equal groups have the same number in every group. We can count in jumps, add the same number again and again, or write it with the × sign: 4 groups of 3 is 4 × 3.

topics: Equal groups and repeated addition (Primary 1, Multiplication and Division 3.1 to 3.4, p. 31)
The multiplication sign × and multiplying within 40
Rows and columns of an array: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. Equal groups, the × sign and multiplying within 40 are in the school Primary 1 syllabus (p. 31), so nothing in this lesson goes beyond Primary 1: products stay within 20 at Start here and within 40 at Go further. The holiday course has no multiplication, so this is new for every child. Reading order (owner default, 22 Oct 2026): "3 groups of 4" is written 3 × 4, groups first, the usual school convention; either order is accepted as correct in an answer, and Think harder shows that 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Sharing and the division sign are Lesson 17, not here. Do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned or syllabus-aligned. Contest tag (tutor only): list all the ways (Think harder T4, Go further G3).

contest_moves: list every way to make equal groups of 12 (T4) and of 24 (G3)
count in jumps instead of one by one
objectives: Say whether groups are equal (the same number in every group) and add counters to make unequal groups equal.
Write "4 groups of 3 = 12" and 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 for a picture or a story, with products to 20.
Write the multiplication sentence 4 × 3 = 12 and read × as "groups of" (the number of groups first, then the number in each group).
Think harder: read an array as rows, turn it and see that 3 × 4 = 4 × 3; find a missing group size in a table of equal groups.
Go further: two kinds of groups in one story (bikes and cars) and totals close to 40.

remember: Count in 2s, 5s and 10s along a number square (Term 1)
Bundles of ten are equal groups: 3 tens and 4 ones (Term 1)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and adding small numbers. Nothing from an earlier lesson is needed: the warm-up counts in jumps along a number square, shows 3 bundles of ten and 4 ones as a picture and makes a ten with two coloured ten-frames. The words group, each and equal and the × sign are taught in Explore and the Mini-lesson.
holiday_topics_revisited: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s (Count with the Frog)
joining_cold.note: Lessons 15 to 18 build on one another (groups, tables, sharing, stories), so try not to miss Lesson 15. A child who misses it watches the recording, does workbook pages 1 and 2 and tells the tutor in the open session. A child who joins at Lesson 16 or later can follow, because that warm-up shows 5 groups of 6 as repeated addition with a picture.

child: The printed workbook, kept flat, with the groups mat (page 6) and the array mat that follows it (nothing to cut)
About 20 small things of one kind (counters, buttons, dry pasta, coins)
4 plates or bowls (paper plates are fine), or use the printed groups mat instead
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
Optional: a muffin tray or an egg box for making rows
tutor: Plates and counters to show on camera if you wish
kit_pages: Groups mat (page 6): six plates to lay counters on. Nothing to cut. Use it if you do not have plates or bowls
Array mat (the next kit page): a grid of squares to lay counters on in rows. Nothing to cut
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears. Nothing in Explore needs more than 20 counters or 4 plates.

timing.notes: Opening is 2 minutes (the routine and rules were taught earlier in the term; give the recording, muting and camera notice). Explore has 14 minutes of plates and counters: equal groups, equal or not, and two ways to see 12. The mini-lesson has 12 because it carries the × sign and the array. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.
skip_order: Start with: cut the Mini-lesson check slide to three sums
Then: shorten Explore round 3 to one way (3 groups of 4)
Then: take the extra minutes from the flex time

sneak_peek.q2: Ben has 4 bags with 3 sweets in each bag. Siti has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag. Who has more sweets? Circle Ben, Siti or Same. Then write or draw how you know.
sneak_peek.a2: Same. Each of them has 12 sweets: 4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4 are both 12.

slides.title: Equal Groups

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Make equal groups and count them fast.

slides.note: Lesson 5 of Term 2, 90 minutes. Objective: make and recognise equal groups, write 4 groups of 3 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12, read an array in rows and see that 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 26, mini-lesson 26 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Say the recording notice in one line: you and the screen only; a child may keep the camera off.
slides.subtitle: Same-size groups, counted fast

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: count in jumps

blocks.text: Touch the yellow numbers as we say them
Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15 ...

items: 2s
5s

slides.note: The yellow numbers are the numbers we say when we count in fives. Count together up to 40, touching each yellow number. Then count in twos (touch every second number) and in tens. Ask: after 25 in fives (30), after 14 in twos (16), after 30 in tens (40). No writing, no marks. A child who is unsure touches each number on the screen.

slides.title: Bundles of ten

blocks.text: Every bundle has the same number of sticks.

items: 2 bundles
3 bundles

slides.note: Each bundle is a ten, so the bundles are equal groups. 3 bundles of ten and 4 singles make 34. Ask: how many sticks in 2 bundles (20), in 3 bundles (30), and what number is 3 tens and 4 ones (34). Children answer aloud or with fingers. A child who has not met tens and ones can count the squares in a bar, then count the bars in jumps.

slides.title: Make a ten

blocks.text: 8 + 6: fill the first frame to make 10, then add the rest.

slides.note: Eight red counters and six yellow counters. Move 2 yellow counters to fill the first frame: that makes 10 and 4 more, so 14. Ask: 9 + 4 (13), 7 + 5 (12), 6 + 8 (14). Children answer aloud. A child who is unsure fills the frame with their own counters. This is the skill we need to add the same number again and again.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Mei puts 2 cookies on each of 3 plates.
How many cookies are there altogether?
You may draw to help.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Ben has 4 bags with 3 sweets in each bag.
Siti has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag.
Who has more sweets? Circle Ben, Siti or Same.
Then write or draw how you know.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (3 plates with 2 cookies on each; 6 cookies) is an access question: any child can count the picture or draw. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: 4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Answers: 6; the same, 12 each. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: equal groups

items: Put 3 counters on each of 4 plates.
Every plate has the same number. The groups are equal.
Count all the counters in jumps of 3.
Now try 5 counters on each of 3 plates.

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Objects first, no writing. Children put 3 counters on each of 4 plates (or on the groups mat), then count them in jumps of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Say the words once: group, each, equal, 4 groups of 3. Then 3 plates with 5 counters each (15). Ask: how many plates, how many on each plate, how many altogether. A child with fewer counters uses 3 plates of 3. The picture shows 4 groups of 3.

slides.title: Are the groups equal?

blocks.text: 1 finger for equal. 2 fingers for not equal.

slides.note: Round 2, about 4 minutes. A is 3 plates of 2 (equal), B is 3, 2 and 3 (not equal), C is 2 plates of 4 (equal). Children show 1 finger for equal and 2 fingers for not equal; do not name a child with a wrong answer. Then children lay out picture B with counters and add counters to make the groups equal: they add 1 counter to the plate with 2. Ask how many more counters they added (1).

slides.title: Two ways to see 12

blocks.text: Use the same 12 counters both times.

slides.note: Round 3, about 4 minutes. Take 12 counters. First make 3 plates with 4 on each (3 groups of 4). Then put the same 12 counters on 4 plates, 3 on each (4 groups of 3). Ask what children notice: the total is the same, 12, but the groups are different. Do not say 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 yet: we see it again with an array in the mini-lesson. Do not say share: the word sharing belongs to Lesson 17.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: What makes groups equal?
How can we count equal groups fast?
What stayed the same when we changed 3 groups of 4 to 4 groups of 3?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: equal groups have the same number in every group; we can count in jumps (3, 6, 9, 12) instead of one by one; the total stayed 12 when we turned 3 groups of 4 into 4 groups of 3. Repeat a child’s answer in your own words so the recording picks it up. Say: next we learn a short way to write it.

slides.title: Groups of
slides.note: Look at 4 plates with 3 cookies on each. We say 4 groups of 3. We can add the same number again and again: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. Point to each plate as you add. Ask: how many groups, how many in each, how many altogether. Say that 4 is the number of groups and 3 is the number in each group.

slides.title: The × sign

blocks.text: × means groups of: the first number is how many groups.

slides.note: The sign × is a short way to write groups of. 4 × 3 means 4 groups of 3. Read it as 4 groups of 3 (or 4 times 3). The first number is how many groups; the second is how many in each group. Reveal the table one row at a time and let children say the total first. Accept 3 × 4 as a correct way to write the same total (we meet this in the array); frames in the workbook use groups first.

slides.title: Equal groups only

cols.text: Equal groups: 3 groups of 3. We can write 3 × 3.
Not equal groups: 3, 2 and 3. We cannot write a × sentence yet.

slides.note: We use × only when every group has the same number. The left picture is 3 groups of 3 (9). The right picture has 3, 2 and 3, so it is not equal groups. Ask: what could we do to make it equal? Add 1 cookie to the plate with 2. This links to the how many more to make equal groups question in Think harder.

slides.title: Rows and columns
slides.note: An array is equal groups in rows. 3 rows with 4 balls in each row is 3 × 4 = 12. Turn the page on its side: now there are 4 rows with 3 in each row, 4 × 3 = 12. The balls are the same, so the total is the same: 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Ask: does the picture work for 2 rows of 5 and 5 rows of 2 (both 10)? Link back to the sneak-peek: 4 bags of 3 and 3 bags of 4.

slides.title: Your turn

blocks.text: Write the sum, the × sentence and the total.

items: 5 groups of 2
2 groups of 6
3 groups of 5
4 groups of 4

slides.note: Each child writes the four totals on their own paper: for example 5 groups of 2 is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10, so 5 × 2 = 10. Walk the cameras; do not ask children to hold papers up. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Answers: 10, 12, 15, 16. Children may use counters or draw groups.

slides.title: Check: groups of
slides.note: Answers: 10, 12, 15, 16. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Children mark their own in another colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Link back: 2 groups of 6 is 6 + 6, a double (Lesson 13).

slides.title: Clap in groups

blocks.text: I say a group. Clap softly in groups and pause.
Say the total out loud together.
Stand up. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call: 2 groups of 3 (clap 3, pause, clap 3: 6), 3 groups of 2 (6), 4 groups of 2 (8), 3 groups of 5 (15). Children clap softly or tap their thighs, pausing between groups, and say the total together. No equipment, no running, a little clear space. A child may stay seated and tap the table.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder. Question 1: equal or not, circle Yes or No. Question 2: a picture of 3 plates, fill in the blanks. Question 3: 5 jars with 2 sweets, add and write groups of.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q1 left Yes, right No; Q2 3 plates, 5 cookies on each plate, 3 groups of 5 = 15; Q3 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 and 5 groups of 2 = 10.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 6. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 4 to 6 aloud. Question 4: draw 4 dots on each plate, then write 3 groups of 4. Question 5: fill in the table of groups, in each and total. Question 6: a story about 4 boxes of pencils; write the number sentence with a sign in the circle, then the answer.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Question 6: the sign in the circle is ×. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q4 3 groups of 4 = 12; Q5 15, 8, 10; Q6 4 × 5 = 20 and 20 pencils.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. Not finished? Pages 3 to 5 are for home too.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: MEI TRIES 2 GROUPS OF 5 AND 5 GROUPS OF 2
items: She says: swap the numbers and the total stays the same.

blocks.text: Is Mei right? How could we be sure?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Children try 2 groups of 5 and 5 groups of 2 with counters, then another pair such as 3 and 6. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: yes for these, both are 10; turn an array of 2 rows of 5 and it becomes 5 rows of 2; test more pairs. Repeat each child’s answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: The same! 12 each. 4 × 3 = 3 × 4.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone’s earlier answer. Ben has 4 groups of 3 and Siti has 3 groups of 4; both are 12 sweets, because turning the groups gives the same total. Puzzle 1: 3 plates with 2 cookies is 6.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back.

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. Read E1, E2 and E3 aloud (the questions are on the slide). Children tick their own ticket against the next slide. Nobody holds paper to the camera and there is no private chat.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children check their own ticket in a different colour. Answers: 20; option 2, 3 + 3 + 3 + 3; the sentence 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 pencils.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide). You then help in the open session next lesson. Never a direct message to a child. The Next time I will try row is optional.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Skip-Count Tables
Have ready: your workbook with the 100 square page, 2 or 3 coloured pencils, about 20 counters, pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional slides and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: what if?

blocks.text: Mei has 3 bags with 5 sweets in each bag. Ali has 5 bags with 3 sweets in each bag.
Who has more sweets?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: the same, 15 each. Turning the groups gives the same total (3 × 5 = 5 × 3). Take two answers and move on. This repeats the sneak-peek idea with new numbers.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Swap two numbers. Does the total stay the same?
Draw equal groups. Ask your grown-up for the total.
Show a toy 3 groups of 5 with counters

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

lines.text: @rec

Hello, inquirers! Please stay muted unless I invite you to speak. Cameras on if you can, so I can see your page and hands; cameras off is fine too. Pencil ready, and your plates, counters and workbook on the table.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. You may mute and keep your camera off.
Today we make equal groups. Equal means the same number in every group. We will count them fast, and we will meet a new sign.
If you can, greet each child by first name before you start the recording. While it runs, avoid names. Check that the page and hands can be seen, or ask the grown-up.

Say the recording notice in the SAY line above in your own words: the recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any unmuted voice; children may mute and keep the camera off. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced earlier in the term: do not re-teach them.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody holds paper to the camera. The first recording of the term shows the full routine.
@rec
Counting in jumps. Touch the yellow numbers as we count in fives: five, ten, fifteen, twenty. Count with me up to forty.
Count in fives. What comes after twenty-five?
Now count in twos: two, four, six, eight. Touch every second number.
What comes after fourteen when we count in twos?
And in tens: ten, twenty, thirty.
What comes after thirty when we count in tens?
Bundles of ten. Every bundle is the same size. Three bundles of ten and four singles make thirty-four.
How many sticks are in two bundles of ten?
How many sticks are in three bundles of ten?
What number is three tens and four ones?
Make a ten. Eight and six. Move two counters to fill the first frame: that is ten, and four more.
Nine plus four?
Seven plus five?
Six plus eight?

If a child is unsure about counting in jumps, touch each number on the screen and count slowly. For bundles, count the squares in one bar, then the bars. For the ten-frame, fill the first frame with counters and count on.

Answers: 30, 16, 40; 20, 30, 34; 13, 12, 14. Children answer with a whisper, fingers or hands. Nobody writes. Do not say multiply yet. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and adding small numbers.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Mei puts 2 cookies on each of 3 plates. How many cookies are there altogether? You may draw to help.
Children draw or count and write the number on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Ben has 4 bags with 3 sweets in each bag. Siti has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag. Who has more sweets? Circle Ben, Siti or Same. Then write or draw how you know.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.

Puzzle 1 answer: 6 cookies. Puzzle 2 answer: the same, 12 sweets each (4 groups of 3 and 3 groups of 4). Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew the bags or counted in jumps). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Your hands are the teachers. Put 3 counters on each of 4 plates. Every plate has the same number: these are equal groups.
Children put 3 counters on each of 4 plates (or on the groups mat).
How many plates? How many counters on each plate?
Count all the counters in jumps of three: three, six, nine, twelve. We say: 4 groups of 3 is 12 altogether.
Children count in threes, touching each plate: 12.
Now put 5 counters on each of 3 plates. How many groups, and how many in each group?
Children make 3 groups of 5.
How many counters are there altogether?
Round two. Are the groups equal? Look at each picture. Show one finger for equal and two fingers for not equal.
Picture A. Equal or not equal?
Picture B. Equal or not equal?
Picture C. Equal or not equal?
Picture B has 3, 2 and 3. Put counters on three plates the same way. Add counters so that every plate has the same number.
Children lay out 3, 2 and 3 and add counters until every plate has 3: they add 1.
How many more counters did you add?
Round three. Take 12 counters. Make 3 plates with 4 counters on each. That is 3 groups of 4.
Children make 3 groups of 4 with 12 counters.
Now put the same 12 counters on 4 plates, with 3 on each. That is 4 groups of 3.
Children make 4 groups of 3 with the same 12 counters.
What do you notice about the total? What changed, and what stayed the same?
What makes groups equal? How can we count equal groups fast?
Equal groups let us count in jumps. Next we learn a short way to write them.

A child who is unsure if groups are equal: count each plate and say the numbers aloud: 3, 2, 3. A child with few counters: use the printed groups mat, or draw circles and dots. A child who counts one by one: show jumps of 3.

Main room only; children say their answers aloud and show fingers; you cannot see builds on small tiles. Answers: 4 groups of 3 is 12; 3 groups of 5 is 15; A equal, B not equal, C equal; 1 more counter; 3 groups of 4 and 4 groups of 3 are both 12. Do not say 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 yet and do not use the word share: it belongs to Lesson 17. Nothing here needs more than 20 counters or 4 plates.
@rec
Look at 4 plates with 3 cookies on each. We say 4 groups of 3. We can add the same number again and again: three plus three plus three plus three is twelve.
How many groups? How many in each group? How many altogether?
There is a short way to write groups of. We use the sign ×. Four times three means 4 groups of 3. The first number is how many groups. The second is how many in each group.
Look at 5 groups of 2. What is the total? How would you write it with the sign?
We use the sign only when every group has the same number. The left picture is equal. The right picture has 3, 2 and 3: not equal groups.
What could we do to make the right picture equal?
Here are 12 balls in rows. 3 rows of 4 is three times four. Turn the page on its side: 4 rows of 3 is four times three. The balls are the same, so the total is the same: twelve.
Does the same work for 2 rows of 5 and 5 rows of 2?
Your turn. Write the sum, the times sentence and the total. 5 groups of 2. 2 groups of 6. 3 groups of 5. 4 groups of 4.
Children write the sum and the total for four groups on their own paper.
Ten. Twelve. Fifteen. Sixteen. Mark your own in another colour.

Key words to use every time: group, each, equal, in all, groups of, times. Do not say that × means multiply by: say groups of. This lesson is within the Primary 1 syllabus (multiplication within 40); keep the pace gentle and use the pictures. Accept 3 × 4 or 4 × 3 as a correct way to write a total in a child’s own work; our frames put the number of groups first.
If a child writes 4 + 3 for 4 groups of 3, ask them to build it: 4 plates, 3 on each. If a child says the groups are equal when they are not, ask them to count each group aloud.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. I say a group. Clap softly in groups, with a pause between groups, and say the total.
Call 2 groups of 3, 3 groups of 2, 4 groups of 2, 3 groups of 5. Children clap softly (or tap their thighs) in groups, pausing between groups, and say the total aloud together.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: are the groups equal? Circle Yes or No for each picture. Question 2: look at the picture and fill in the blanks. Question 3: Mei has 5 jars. Each jar has 2 sweets. Fill in the blanks.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Question 1: left, yes. Right, no. Question 2: 3 plates, 5 cookies on each plate, 3 groups of 5 is 15. Question 3: ten, ten, and ten sweets in all. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: draw 4 dots on each plate, then fill in the blank. Question 5: fill in the table. Question 6: Aisha has 4 boxes. Each box has 5 pencils. Write a number sentence with a sign in the circle, then fill in the blank.
Page 2, questions 4 to 6.
Question 4: 3 groups of 4 is 12. Question 5: 15, 8, 10. Question 6: 4 times 5 is 20, and Aisha has 20 pencils.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time. Anything not finished is for home too.
Stand and stretch for 30 seconds, then sit down and choose.

Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page. If Start here took the whole time, say that pages 3 to 5 are for home, and keep the time.

start.text: Are the groups equal? Circle Yes or No for each picture.
start.hint: Count what is in each group. Are all the groups the same?
start.solution: The left picture has 3 bags with 4 sweets in each bag: the groups are equal. The right picture has 2, 3 and 2 cookies: the groups are not equal.
mistakes: Counting only the number of groups.
Saying Yes because the pictures look alike.

start.text: Look at the picture. Fill in the blanks.

parts.text: There are [] cookies on each plate.

start.answer: 3 plates; 5 cookies on each plate; 3 groups of 5 = 15
start.hint: Count the plates. Then count the cookies on one plate.
start.solution: There are 3 plates and each plate has 5 cookies. 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so 3 groups of 5 = 15.
mistakes: Counting the cookies on every plate and losing count.

start.text: Mei has 5 jars. Each jar has 2 sweets. How many sweets does Mei have in all?
start.hint: Add 2 again and again, or count in twos.
start.solution: 5 jars with 2 sweets each: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. So 5 groups of 2 = 10 and Mei has 10 sweets in all.

start.text: Draw 4 dots on each plate. Then fill in the blank.
start.hint: Draw 4 dots on one plate. Then draw 4 dots on each of the other plates.
start.solution: 3 plates with 4 dots on each: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, so 3 groups of 4 = 12.
mistakes: Drawing different numbers of dots on the plates.

start.hint: The first number is how many groups. The second is how many in each group.
start.solution: 3 groups of 5 = 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. 4 groups of 2 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. 2 groups of 5 = 5 + 5 = 10.
mistakes: Writing the number of groups in the Total box.

start.text: Aisha has 4 boxes. Each box has 5 pencils. How many pencils does Aisha have in all?
start.hint: Write the number of boxes first. Then write the number of pencils in each box.
start.solution: 4 boxes with 5 pencils in each box. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. The number sentence is 4 × 5 = 20 and Aisha has 20 pencils.

think.text: Look at the dots in rows. Fill in the blanks.

parts.text: Turn the picture on its side. [] × [] = [2]

think.hint: Count the rows. Then count the dots in one row.
think.solution: The picture has 3 rows with 4 dots in each row: 3 × 4 = 12. Turned on its side it has 4 rows with 3 dots in each row: 4 × 3 = 12. The totals are the same, so 3 × 4 = 4 × 3.
mistakes: Thinking the totals must be different because the pictures look different.

think.text: Each plate should have 3 cookies. Look at the picture. How many more cookies are needed to make the groups equal?
think.hint: Count the cookies on each plate. How many are missing from each plate?
think.solution: The plates have 3, 1 and 2 cookies. The second plate needs 2 more and the third plate needs 1 more. 2 + 1 = 3 more cookies.
mistakes: Adding only the missing cookies of one plate.

think.text: Kumar has 3 plates with 4 apples on each plate. He says he has 7 apples.

parts.text: Is Kumar correct? Circle Yes or No.

think.hint: Add the apples on the 3 plates: 4 + 4 + 4.
think.solution: 3 groups of 4 apples: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. 7 is 3 + 4, which is not the same as 3 groups of 4. So Kumar is not correct.

think.text: Jenny has 12 stickers. She puts them into equal groups in different ways. Fill in the table.
think.hint: Count in jumps. For example, how many jumps of 3 make 12?
think.solution: 4 groups of 3 = 12, so each of the 4 groups has 3. 3 groups of 4 = 12, so the number of groups is 3.
mistakes: Writing the total in every box.
Choosing numbers that do not make 12.

go.text: A shed has 3 bikes and 4 cars. Each bike has 2 wheels. Each car has 4 wheels. How many wheels are there in all?
go.hint: First find the wheels on the bikes. Then find the wheels on the cars.
go.solution: 3 bikes have 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 wheels. 4 cars have 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 wheels. 6 + 16 = 22 wheels in all.
mistakes: Forgetting to add the wheels of the bikes and the cars.

go.text: Jamie has 6 jars. Each jar has 5 marbles. Jamie needs 40 marbles. How many more marbles does he need?
go.hint: Find how many marbles are in the jars now. Then see how many more make 40.
go.solution: 6 jars with 5 marbles in each jar: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 30 marbles. 40 - 30 = 10 more marbles.

go.text: Wei has 24 sweets. Show 3 different ways to put them into equal groups. Many answers are right.
go.answer: For example 2 groups of 12, 3 groups of 8, 4 groups of 6 (also 6 of 4, 8 of 3, 12 of 2, 1 of 24, 24 of 1)
go.hint: Try counting in jumps: 4, 8, 12 ... or 6, 12, 18 ... Do the jumps land on 24?
mistakes: Choosing numbers that do not make 24.

investigation.title: Rows with 12 counters
investigation.first: Put 12 counters in 2 rows of 6. Turn the grid on its side. How many rows now?
investigation.text: Use 12 counters. Make rows and columns in different ways, for example 3 rows of 4. Write the × sentence for each. Try 5 rows. Does it work?
investigation.answer: Six ways: 1 × 12, 2 × 6, 3 × 4, 4 × 3, 6 × 2 and 12 × 1. Turning a picture gives a second one (2 × 6 and 6 × 2). 5 rows does not work: 5 rows of 2 uses 10 counters and 2 are left over.
investigation.look_for: A child who builds several arrays, writes a × sentence for each and notices that turning one gives another. Credit a child who tries 5 rows and finds counters left over. Do not mark a child down for finding only three ways.
mistakes: Counting the same picture twice (2 × 6 and 6 × 2 are the same counters turned, but both are good sentences).

talk.question: Mei tries 2 groups of 5 and 5 groups of 2. She says: swap the numbers and the total stays the same. Is Mei right? How could we be sure?
talk.answer: Yes for these: both are 10. We can turn an array of 2 rows of 5 and get 5 rows of 2. A few tests are good evidence; the picture of the same counters in rows and columns shows why.
talk.look_for: A child who says test more pairs, or who turns an array or draws it both ways. Not just "yes" or "no".

exit.text: Which is the same as 4 groups of 3? Write its number in the bracket.
Ali has 3 boxes. Each box has 4 pencils. How many pencils does Ali have in all?
exit.solution: 3 boxes with 4 pencils in each box: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The sign in the circle is ×.

home_practice.text: Ali puts 3 sweets on each of 4 plates. Fill in the blanks. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = [2]  4 groups of 3 = [2]
Mei has 2 bags with 3 sweets in each bag and 1 bag with 4 sweets. Are the groups equal? Circle Yes or No.
home_practice.solution: The bags have 3, 3 and 4 sweets. The groups are not equal.

home_practice.text: Fill in the blanks. 5 + 5 + 5 = [2]  3 groups of 5 = [2]  3 × 5 = [2]
home_practice.solution: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. 3 groups of 5 and 3 × 5 mean the same: 15.

home_practice.text: Is 2 × 6 = 6 × 2? Circle Yes or No. Use 12 counters or draw dots to check.
home_practice.solution: 2 rows of 6 is 12 and 6 rows of 2 is 12, so the totals are the same.

home_practice.text: A tricycle has 3 wheels. A bike has 2 wheels. How many wheels do 4 tricycles and 3 bikes have in all? ___ wheels

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask ‘How do you know?’ and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: swap the two numbers and the total stays the same. Test 2 groups of 7 and 7 groups of 2, then 4 groups of 5 and 5 groups of 4. Can you find a pair that breaks it?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Test 2 groups of 7 with 7 groups of 2, and 4 groups of 5 with 5 groups of 4.
menu.answer: 14 and 14; 20 and 20. No pair breaks it: turning the same counters in rows and columns never changes the total.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Draw 3 or 4 plates with the same number of dots on each plate. Ask your grown-up: how many dots altogether? Then count in jumps together to check.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Draw equal groups. Ask a grown-up how many in all, then check by counting in jumps.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check that the groups are equal and that the total is the number of groups times the number in each group.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen equal groups. Show them 3 groups of 5 with counters and tell them how many altogether.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Show a grown-up 3 groups of 5 with counters and say how many in all.
menu.answer: 3 groups of 5: 5, 10, 15. There are 15 counters altogether. 3 × 5 = 15.

parent.summary: We made equal groups with plates and counters. Equal means the same number in every group. We counted in jumps, added the same number again and again (3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12) and met the × sign: 4 groups of 3 is 4 × 3. Rows of dots showed that 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 make the same total. Equal groups and × are Primary 1 work at school; we start from objects and pictures.
words: equal groups: the same number in every group
in each: how many in one group
try_home: Plates: put 3 small things on each of 4 plates. How many altogether? Count in jumps of 3. Keep small things away from mouths.
Equal or not? Make 3 groups with 3, 2 and 3 things. How many more make them equal?
Turn it: make 2 rows of 5 buttons. Turn the tray. How many rows now? Does the total change?
ask: How many groups? How many in each group?
Are all the groups equal? How do you know?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use counters on plates or draw dots, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking ‘how many in each group?’ works better than giving the answer. If the look-back page says ‘I am still stuck’, photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept 90 days after the program ends.
parent.next: Lesson 16: Skip-Count Tables. Online practice: your tutor will share the practice link.
parent.quote: Equal groups can be counted fast: count in jumps and write it with ×.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to see equal groups, count them fast and write them with the × sign. This week: equal groups, repeated addition and 4 groups of 3 = 4 × 3.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to draw a story, to use groups and sharing, and to test a claim with an example.

safeguarding: Counters and small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Keep small things away from younger brothers and sisters. Use paper plates or the printed groups mat rather than glass or china.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or a board up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on a count of three, or show fingers for a choice. There is no private chat.

Never read out a child’s name with a right or wrong answer. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. A child’s page is never shown.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. Clapping is soft; a child may stay seated and tap the table.

A child who is still stuck ticks ‘I am still stuck’ on the look-back page. A grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp only; photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends. The tutor then helps in the open session next lesson. No private messages to children, and no personal phones.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first. Check the Think harder table (T4) and the Go further totals (22 wheels, 30 marbles) so you can answer a child who finds another way to make 24.
Tell parents a week before: print the workbook pages and the kit pages (nothing to cut), and find 4 plates or bowls and about 20 small things. Small things stay away from mouths and younger children.
Have the slides open and check the groups mat is visible on screen share. Have 4 plates and counters to show on camera if you wish.
Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children’s video is excluded; any unmuted voice is recorded. Start the recording after the greeting, and avoid first names while it runs.

Read groups of as number of groups first: 4 groups of 3 is 4 × 3. Accept 3 × 4 as a correct way to write the same total in a child’s own work. Say plainly to families that equal groups and × are Primary 1 work. Do not call the lesson MOE-aligned. Lessons 15 to 18 build on one another.
